title: Independence and the Product Test
quickIdea: A and B are independent exactly when P(A and B) = P(A)P(B), equivalently P(A|B) = P(A) whenever P(B) > 0. The test is the product, computed on the numbers in the question - never read off the story.
remember: The product form is the definition, because it needs no positivity assumption and is visibly symmetric in A and B.
Independence of A and B carries to A^c and B, to A and B^c, and to A^c and B^c. All four products hold together, so one of them failing is enough to disprove independence.
Compute both sides with the given numbers. A story that sounds unrelated proves nothing; a story that sounds connected proves nothing either.
Independence is a statement about probabilities, not about causation: two events can be independent through cancellation of causes.
P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B) are equivalent when both conditionals exist, so either form may be used as the test.
For three or more events the pairwise products are not enough; mutual independence needs the higher-order products as well, which is the next card.

example.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. A = head on both, B = head on the first, C = head on the second. Test each pair for independence.
example.work: The space is HH, HT, TH, TT. P(A) = 1/4, P(B) = 1/2, P(C) = 1/2. P(A and B) = 1/4 (only HH), while P(A)P(B) = 1/8: not independent. P(A and C) = 1/4 against 1/8: not independent. P(B and C) = 1/4 = (1/2)(1/2): independent. And P(B|C) = (1/4)/(1/2) = 1/2 = P(B), which is the same statement.
example.answer: B and C are independent; A is dependent on each of them.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2023 Q.43 asks exactly these four verdicts as an MSQ, and the two true statements are C and D - the independent pair, and the conditional form of the same fact.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2023 Q.43: two fair coins are tossed. A = head on both throws, B = head on the first throw, C = head on the second throw. Which are true? (A) A and B independent. (B) A and C independent. (C) B and C independent. (D) P(B|C) = P(B).
variations.why: P(B and C) = 1/4 = P(B)P(C) and P(B|C) = 1/2 = P(B). For A the joint probabilities are 1/4 against a product of 1/8, so A is dependent on both.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: If A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.6 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A^c and B)?
variations.why: A^c and B are independent too, so P(A^c and B) = (1 - 0.6)(0.5) = 0.2. The complement carries independence with it.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5, P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent, and what is P(A|B)?
variations.why: The two tests are the same test; this variation makes the equivalence visible on a single pair of numbers.

trap.what: Deciding independence from the wording of the question instead of from the product.
trap.why: Independence is a numerical relation between three probabilities. Two events in the same experiment can be independent, and two events in different experiments can fail to be independent if they are tied together by a condition.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2023 Q.43, 'head on both' sounds like it should depend on 'head on the first', and it does - but the same experiment's two single-coin events are independent, which is equally counter-intuitive until the products are written down.

check.question: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A and B) = 0.2. Are A and B independent?
check.explanation: P(A)P(B) = 0.4 x 0.5 = 0.2, which equals P(A and B), so the product test passes.
